item.title: Protecting small businesses from extortion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest reporting on extortion in Dhaka’s markets reveals a crisis that has gone on for far too long and one that must be taken seriously.
Small traders are the backbone of our capital’s daily economy but are being squeezed by criminal groups, politically-connected operatives, and local strongmen who demand payments simply for the “right” to operate.
At a time when everyday people are struggling due to numerous economic challenges, that these small traders and businesses are having to experience this is distressing, to say the least.
That a systematic pattern of intimidation exists that is draining livelihoods, raising prices for consumers, and eroding public trust in law enforcement should alarm the authorities and compel them to take action with immediate effect.
Many traders pay because the alternative is violence, vandalism, or being forced out of business entirely. Some have already shut down operations, unable to survive the pressure.
We must also recognize that this is not merely a law‑and‑order issue but also an economic threat. When small traders are extorted, the entire supply chain suffers. Prices rise, competition shrinks, and honest businesses lose ground to those protected by criminal networks.
Authorities cannot pretend this is invisible any longer. Enforcement remains sporadic, and crackdowns rarely dismantle the networks behind the extortion. We agree with experts on the matter that a few arrests will not solve a problem that is deeply entrenched.
What is needed is a sustained, uncompromising campaign against extortion. Police must protect traders, not leave them to negotiate with criminals while market committees must be held accountable when they enable or ignore illegal collections.
Most importantly, we need our political leadership to make it clear that extortion will be met with decisive action and not just empty promises.
Small traders keep Dhaka running and they have earned the right to safety, dignity, and the freedom to work without fear. It is time for the authorities to prove that the city belongs to its citizens, not to those who prey on them.

item.title: Preserving our harvest. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The near‑completion of a modern cold storage facility in Bandarban is undeniably good news. Farmers lose large portions of their seasonal fruits and vegetables every year due to inadequate storage in our country. To combat this loss, cold storage facilities are nothing if not a lifeline.
However, there is a truth we cannot deny: Bangladesh needs many more such facilities, and it needs them fast.
Bangladesh’s farmers have long been forced into distress sales, watching their produce spoil before reaching the market. A 50‑metric‑ton cold storage, now 95% complete, will certainly go a long way to help preserve their harvest and potentially reduce post‑harvest losses, protect incomes, and give growers the confidence to expand cultivation.
For a district with enormous untapped potential, this could be transformative for its farmers.
However, the fact is that Bangladesh’s agricultural infrastructure remains very uneven. In too many districts, farmers still rely on makeshift sheds, improvised cooling, or no storage at all. As a result, bumper harvests often turn into financial disappointment.
We may speak of boosting exports, diversifying crops, and strengthening food security, but without modern storage facilities, these ambitions remain fragile.
The Bandarban facility should therefore be seen as the beginning of a nationwide push to modernize post‑harvest infrastructure.
Every major producing district needs cold storage that matches its output. Farmers deserve to have access to reliable preservation so they are not forced to sell at throwaway prices every year.
For a robust future where we can tackle growing threats of food security, it is simply not enough to depend on what our farmers can grow. We must be able to preserve our harvest.

item.title: On London's Brick Lane, a data centre sparks local battle. [ dawn ]
item.description:
In Brick Lane, the historic heart of London’s Bangladeshi community, residents oppose plans for a data centre in a disused brewery, citing the erosion of heritage and need for social housing.

“This has really been the focal point of the British Bangladeshi community,” local councillor Faysal Ahmed told AFP, recalling a time when his parents ran a restaurant beneath his childhood home in the Lane.

While many curry houses remain, the street and the surrounding neighbourhood is transforming, in part to help power the capital’s digital infrastructure boom.

Part of a multi-million pound redevelopment of the sprawling former Truman brewery site, the East End financial data centre is an unlikely addition to the graffiti-lined Brick Lane, where tourists spill between vintage shops and queue for bagels served through the night.

The 10-acre site will also be transformed by new offices and retail space, primarily serving the neighbouring financial district filled with skyscrapers.

Approval of the development by the UK government comes as a boom in water- and energy-hungry data centres — particularly as demand rises for facilities supporting artificial intelligence — fuels local opposition worldwide.

For Ahmed, the development uses land that could help house some of the roughly 31,000 residents on the waiting list for social housing in the Tower Hamlets district.

The redevelopment plans are for only 44 flats, including just six for social housing, prompting residents to recently protest outside the Ministry of Housing.

‘Preserving heritage’

“My personal concern is about the need for affordable social housing for young people and preserving the heritage, the special character, of the area,” said Susanna Kow, a member of the Save Brick Lane campaign.

According to planning documents, the Labour government gave “significant weight” to the benefits of additional data centre capacity, citing the need to “meet the escalating demand driving emerging technologies such as AI and increased digital services”.

The government’s housing department declined to comment on its decision in August to approve the plans, while the Truman Brewery has not responded to an AFP request for its reaction.

“We’ve been campaigning on planning issues and… the incursion of the city on the East End for quite a number of years,” said Jonathan Moberly, who is leading local opposition.

He said the project was part of a “growing national issue about the amount of power taken from the grid that can stop other developments happening, like housing”.

The International Energy Agency in April reported that the global electricity demand of data centres grew by 17 per cent last year.

It projects the electricity consumption from these centres will double over the next five years to 2030.

“The UK already faces a projected daily water deficit of nearly five billion litres by 2050,” according to a report on the UK government website.

“National water resource plans… do not adequately account for the burgeoning demand from infrastructure such as AI data centres. This oversight risks intensifying water stress in already vulnerable regions.”

‘Trojan horse’

For industry consultant Mark Acton, the infrastructure is increasingly essential, particularly in London, a city where proximity can provide the ultra-fast response times needed for financial trading.

“Everything we currently do digitally comes from a data centre,” said Acton, who argued the facilities have become an easy target owing to what he said was a lack of understanding of their actual water and energy use.

If Britain is serious about sovereignty over its AI infrastructure, “you’ve got to have somewhere to put it”, Acton said.

But campaigners at environmental charity Global Action Plan argue that UK planning rules have not kept pace with the expansion of the sector or adequately accounted for environmental costs.

“It’s been a kind of Trojan horse for bad development,” Owen Espley, the group’s community campaigns manager, told AFP.

“We need local knowledge and input to go into shaping developments to improve them and make sure that we get better data centres at the end of it,” he said.

Further down Brick Lane, Carol Burns, born and raised in the area, has no intention of going anywhere.

Sitting inside the shop her family has run since the 1800s — its walls covered with family photographs — Burns is proud to be part of London’s East End community.

“People are always trying to buy this place, but no. They’ll have to drag me out of here feet-first,” she said in her thick Cockney accent.

item.title: The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit. [ chathamhouse ]
item.description:
The India–China reset will continue at the BRICS summit Expert comment jon.wallace 8 September 2026

So will disagreement over the purpose of BRICS.

India will host the 18th BRICS summit in New Delhi on 12–13 September at a time when the rest of the world is increasingly seeking to emulate its longstanding policy of strategic autonomy.

The Ukraine and Iran wars, continuing US–China rivalry, and the second administration of President Donald Trump have made New Delhi’s long-held commitment to strategic hedging and middle power diplomacy seem wise, if not urgent underpinnings for modern international relations.

However, even though the world may better reflect India’s worldview, New Delhi has found it difficult to apply its foreign policy approach to its BRICS chairmanship. 

Strain with Washington, reengagement with Moscow and Beijing

Recent Indian government actions confirm India’s continuing commitment to strategic hedging. New Delhi secured a string of resource deals during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s recent visits to Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan. And it has agreed a number of trade deals, with nine in-progress or concluded since 2021 – including with the United Kingdom and European Union.

Trade negotiations with the United States continue, but relations with the second Trump administration have undoubtedly been strained, causing India to reinvest in other relationships.

Ony a few years ago, India was distancing itself from the China-led Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO): New Delhi hosted a low-key virtual summit in 2023. And Modi was absent from the summit in 2024. But more recently India has renewed its interest in the grouping and sought to improve relations with China and Russia. At this year’s SCO summit, Modi joined President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin in signing the Bishkek Declaration, which condemned US-Israeli military attacks on Iran.

India’s BRICS agenda

India has consistently sought to be a ‘voice’ of the Global South, often by using its prominent position in platforms like the G20 (which it chaired in 2023) and the AI Impact Summit (which it hosted earlier this year).

Its BRICS chairmanship has continued these efforts. In August a joint declaration, the ‘Chennai Consensus’ made a commitment to collaborative research and innovation among developing countries on emerging technologies. The same month, BRICS trade ministers advocated preserving and revitalizing the multilateral trading system – a move likely aimed at the Trump administration’s disruptive tariff policies. And in June, BRICS agriculture ministers issued a food security declaration focused on the needs of developing countries.

The challenge for New Delhi is that it wishes to promote this worldview in a way that is non-Western but not explicitly anti-Western. To that end, it has sought to downplay some of the more controversial elements of the BRICS agenda. That includes a de-dollarization narrative championed by countries such as Brazil and Russia – an idea which last year caused President Trump to threaten to slap ten per cent tariffs on the BRICS in response.

Related work

How China–India relations will shape Asia and the global order

New Delhi emphasized that BRICS is not seeking to create a separate reserve currency to compete with the US dollar. It has instead reframed this as an effort to settle bilateral trade in national currencies and use digital payments to reduce transaction costs for cross-border trade.

India has also promoted a more benign worldview, reflected in the BRICS slogan of ‘Humanity First’ and the theme of ‘Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability’. But this seems increasingly outdated given recent geopolitical developments, in particular US military action against Venezuela and Iran.

India’s position can appear out of sync in a forum whose membership includes countries with more overtly anti-Western agendas, including China, Russia and Iran. And two other BRICS countries, South Africa and Brazil, have suffered high profile diplomatic disputes with the US.

A key watchpoint at this summit will therefore be how New Delhi reconciles its efforts to stay on good terms with Washington with calls by BRICS member states to voice opposition to US actions. As Chair and host of BRICS, India’s actions will be more scrutinized, and it will be reluctant to oversee the production of a statement similar to Bishkek. 

Multilateral symbolism

These tensions are exacerbated by the broader challenges of maintaining cohesion among the 11 BRICS member states. Tensions between Iran and the UAE, for instance, are high as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Relations between Addis Ababa and Cairo have been strained by Ethiopia’s Nile dam project. Saudi and UAE interests conflict on relations with Israel and other issues. And India has its own longstanding frictions with China to manage, although there have been signs of improvement over the last two years.

Additionally, among the founding member states – Brazil, Russia, India, and China – there is still no consensus on what the BRICS stands for. Brazil and India see it primarily as an economic-driven initiative. China and Russia see it through more of a geopolitical lens. Beijing in particular is increasingly using forums like the BRICS to promote its own worldviews through its Global Development, Security, Civilization and Governance Initiatives. Meanwhile, Moscow has used the BRICS to seek alignment with the Global South as it is ostracized by the West following its invasion of Ukraine.

From New Delhi’s perspective, BRICS has been moving in the wrong direction. BRICS was established as a reaction to calls for a greater voice for the Global South in multilateral institutions, with a focus on development and governance. India would like to build on the organization’s earlier achievements, including the establishment of the BRICS New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement in 2015.

The difficulties BRICS has speaking with one voice could affect its future. In the two decades since the BRICS was formed, newer groupings have emerged, such as the recent defence pact between Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia. There is a possibility that such regional, exclusive groupings may become more important actors than expansive and inclusive groupings like BRICS.

Such factors mean that BRICS expansion is likely to take a backseat for the foreseeable future. Instead, the focus will probably be on socializing new members into the organization.

Efforts to expand the BRICS mandate will likely be limited to engagement with other forums in the Global South. However, even this is challenging. Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rehman – whose country holds the chair of BIMSTEC, a South and Southeast Asian regional forum – has not yet accepted an invitation amid tensions with India.

Bilateral substance

The real action at the BRICS Summit will take place on its sidelines with a series of bilateral meetings. In particular, the meeting between Modi and Xi is likely to further advance the ongoing reset in bilateral relations and build confidence. A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister and Indian national security advisor made notable progress on their longstanding border dispute. And Xi’s upcoming visit to India – his first since 2019 – will reportedly include a 400-person delegation.

In this context, the recent accomplishments of BRICS have come from its convening power. It was a Modi–Xi meeting at the 2024 BRICS Summit in Russia that set the ball rolling on resetting the relationship.

Ultimately, the Global South remains an amorphous concept. There remains little clarity on what advocating its interests actually means, beyond making vague calls for a more equitable distribution of power in a multipolar global order. The BRICS summits needs to move behind platitudes and statements towards more substantive outcomes if it is to be seen as a real contender in global governance.

At the summit, New Delhi will seek to return BRICS to its original development-focused agenda, as reflected in its Economic Partnership Strategy 2030. However, this threatens to be hijacked by fissures among its members and calls for another statement condemning US attacks on Iran. But the group needs more than opposition to the US to define a better vision for the Global South. This entails moving beyond what it stands against to what it stands for.

item.title: Bangladesh’s literacy future begins before first grade. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On the 60th anniversary of International Literacy Day, Bangladesh stands at an important point in its education journey. According to the Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023: Key Findings report, the national literacy rate among people aged seven and above rose to 77.9%, from 58.6% in 2014.
Yet these gains do not tell the whole story. Functional literacy, the ability to read, write, think critically, and apply knowledge in daily life, remains out of reach for millions.
According to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index 2020, 58% of 10-year-olds in Bangladesh are unable to read and understand a simple text by the end of primary school.
That is more than one in every two children.
One important part of this challenge begins even before children enter primary school.
A study by Nirmala, Umayahara, Yang and Ranganathan (2021) shows that up to 80-85% of children from the poorest socioeconomic quintiles enter Class 1 without adequate pre-literacy exposure, structured storytelling, or formal early childhood education.
When children enter primary school without these foundations, they are expected to cope immediately with a fast-paced curriculum. This can lead to early frustration and poor comprehension.
Children from disadvantaged backgrounds are three times more likely to drop out of primary school than their wealthiest peers. This, in turn, can reinforce an intergenerational cycle of poverty and weaken the country’s human resources.
The gap is even wider for children with disabilities. They often face multiple barriers, including negative attitudes, delayed enrolment, and a lack of adapted learning materials. These obstacles can exclude them from the literacy journey before it has properly begun.
Children do not all learn and develop at the same pace or in the same way. Using fixed developmental milestones to decide whether a child is “ready” for school can unfairly disadvantage children with disabilities. Yet with appropriate support, every child can learn and participate.
Early lessons from the GPE KIX- and IDRC Canada-supported EN-REACH Education implementation research project, being conducted in selected government primary schools in Kushtia and Gaibandha districts, suggest that school readiness cannot be strengthened by focusing on the child alone.
The support surrounding the child, particularly from teachers, parents, and other caregivers, also matters.
Preliminary qualitative findings suggest that children with disabilities who were initially shy or anxious became more confident and engaged when they experienced language-rich, play-based learning at home and in school.
Teachers also reported that inclusive, play-based approaches designed to support children with disabilities benefited other children in the classroom as well.
The research is also showing the value of equipping pre-primary teachers with practical skills for inclusive teaching and of using low-cost, locally-available play materials.
At home, involving fathers, grandparents, and community members in school-readiness activities can broaden responsibility for early learning and help build a more supportive and gender-equitable environment for children.
These emerging lessons point to a wider conclusion: Inclusive pre-primary education works best when the classroom, home, and community reinforce one another, rather than when school readiness is treated solely as the responsibility of the child or teacher.
But promising approaches in a few settings will not be enough unless quality pre-primary education becomes more widely accessible. Across Bangladesh, access to quality early education remains deeply unequal.
First , Bangladesh needs to invest more in early education. Expanding preschool enrollment in low- and middle-income countries could generate benefit-to-cost ratios ranging from 6.4 to 17.6.
Yet Bangladesh spends just over 2% of GDP on education, well below Unesco’s recommended 4% to 6%. A significant, protected share of increased education spending should go to pre-primary education in marginalized communities.
Second , inclusion and play-based learning need to become central to pre-primary education.
Classrooms should have age-appropriate reading materials in children’s mother tongues, interactive toys, and storybooks. Pre-primary education should also move away from excessive memorization and give children more opportunities to learn through play, stories, interaction, and exploration.
Third , the pre-primary workforce needs to be professionalized. Teaching young children, particularly children with disabilities, requires specialized pedagogical skills. This should receive proper attention in education planning, budgeting and implementation.
Finally , evidence-based inclusive models need to be scaled up. As stronger evidence emerges on effective ways to include children with disabilities and engage fathers in early learning, the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education, the National Curriculum and Textbook Board, and development partners should consider how these practices can be incorporated into national policy.
If Bangladesh wants a population capable of succeeding in a digital economy, participating meaningfully in society and escaping poverty, investment must begin when the human brain is developing most rapidly.
By ensuring universal, high-quality, play-based and inclusive pre-primary education for every child, Bangladesh can make sure that improvements in literacy are not simply reflected in statistics, but in the knowledge, skills and opportunities of its people.
Utpal Mallick is an Assistant Program Manager at icddr,b and can be reached at utpal.mallick@icddrb.org .

item.title: From a refugee camp in Cox’s Bazar to New York University. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When I fled Myanmar in 2017, I carried very little with me. My family escaped violence, persecution, and fear.
We walked for days through forests and mountains before reaching Bangladesh. Along the way, we lost our home, our security, and the future we had imagined.
But there was one thing I refused to leave behind: My belief in education.
Today, on World Literacy Day, we often think about literacy as the ability to read and write. For refugees, it means much more.
Literacy can mean understanding your rights, accessing reliable information, communicating with the world beyond a refugee camp, challenging misinformation, and finding the confidence to speak for yourself.
For me, education became one of the most powerful forms of protection.
As a Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh, I watched thousands of young people grow up with extremely limited access to formal education. They had dreams of becoming doctors, teachers, engineers, lawyers, and community leaders.
Displacement did not take away their talent or ambition. It took away their opportunities.
This distinction matters.
Refugees do not choose to become refugees. No child chooses to flee war, persecution, or violence. Yet once displaced, refugee children are often expected to carry the consequences of decisions they never made.
They encounter restrictions on movement, lack of legal documentation, poverty, discrimination, language barriers, and limited pathways to higher education.
The result is not simply an education crisis. It is a loss of human potential.
When a young person spends years in a refugee camp without meaningful access to education, we should not ask why that person has failed to progress. We should ask why the systems around them failed to provide an opportunity.
I know what that feels like.
For years, I tried to find a way to continue my education while living as a stateless Rohingya refugee in Bangladesh. There were moments when the possibility of attending a university seemed almost impossible.
I had the desire to learn. I was willing to work. What I did not have was the legal status and opportunity that most students take for granted.
Yet I continued.
In 2024, after seven years as a refugee in Bangladesh, I came to the United States as a student. This year, I graduated from New York University with a bachelor's degree in social science, concentrating in international studies.
My journey from a refugee camp in Cox's Bazar to a university classroom in New York has taught me something important: Talent is universal, but opportunity is not.
I am not the only Rohingya young person capable of reaching a university. There are students in the refugee camps today who could become doctors, lawyers, teachers, entrepreneurs, researchers, diplomats, and leaders.
But talent cannot substitute indefinitely for access.
Through the Rohingya Student Network, which I founded while living in the refugee camp, I have seen what happens when young people are given opportunities to learn.
Education does more than transfer knowledge. It builds confidence. It develops leadership. It gives people the tools to understand the forces shaping their lives and the ability to participate in decisions about their future.
That is why literacy should also be understood as a question of power.
A person who can access information, evaluate it critically, understand their rights, communicate their ideas, and tell their own story is harder to silence.
For a stateless community whose identity and history have repeatedly been denied or misrepresented, that matters enormously.
Literacy also matters in the digital age. Refugees increasingly receive news, communicate, organize, study, and understand events through phones and social media.
Being literate today therefore requires more than reading words on a page. Young people must also be able to distinguish information from misinformation, understand how digital platforms influence what they see, and use technology responsibly.
For the Rohingya, these skills are particularly important. We have already witnessed the devastating consequences of misinformation, hate speech, and dehumanizing narratives.
Education must therefore prepare young people not only for employment but also to think critically, challenge hatred, engage peacefully with others, and become responsible participants in their communities.
The international community often speaks about durable solutions for refugees. Education must be at the centre of that conversation.
Investing in refugee education is not charity. It is one of the smartest investments governments, universities, and donors can make in human potential.
Educated refugees contribute to economies, strengthen communities, promote social cohesion, and help build peace.
They become problem-solvers rather than being viewed solely through the lens of humanitarian need.
My life changed because people and institutions eventually saw beyond my refugee status and recognized my potential as a student. That should not be an exceptional story.
On this World Literacy Day, I hope we move beyond asking how many refugee children can read and write. We should ask a much bigger question: How many have been given the education necessary to determine their own future?
Food keeps people alive. Shelter provides safety. Humanitarian assistance helps people survive displacement.
But education gives people the tools to move beyond survival.
For a refugee, a book can be more than a book. A classroom can be more than a classroom. And literacy can be more than the ability to read and write.
It can be the beginning of freedom.
Maung Sawyedollah is a Rohingya student and activist currently living in New York City. He graduated from New York University this spring with a BA in social science and is currently preparing to start a JD.
